problem_statement: The paper frames European option pricing as a financially important derivative-pricing problem whose payoff depends on the stochastic evolution of asset prices. It says that more realistic pricing requires handling stochastic fluctuations beyond the simplified Black-Scholes-Merton model, and that numerical methods are used to estimate the expected payoff.
problem_statement_quotes: The pricing of financial derivatives is a prominent problem that requires extensive computational resources, as the stochastic nature of the underlying assets requires precise modeling.

One of the typical financial derivatives is the option, which is a contract that allows the holder to buy or sell assets at a pre-established price (strike) at or before a specified date (maturity date).
The payoff of an option relies heavily on the stochastic evolution of asset price.
As such, numerical methods such as the Monte Carlo method are typically employed for handling more realistic stochastic fluctuations.
classical_baseline: The paper treats the Black-Scholes-Merton model as the traditional analytical baseline, and Monte Carlo simulation as the standard numerical baseline for more realistic option pricing. It also contrasts its approach with classical sampling on a computer.
classical_baseline_quotes: The traditional option pricing model, Black-Scholes-Merton model (BSM) [1] usually oversimplifies market dynamics, which limits its practical application to real-life scenarios.

classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical challenge is that option pricing needs extensive computation because the underlying asset is stochastic, Monte Carlo is slow for complicated options, and the BSM model is too simplified for real markets. It also states that more practical cases may not have analytical solutions and that numerical simulation is costly.

business_stakes: The paper says that reducing computational resources and speeding up option pricing could matter for the financial industry, and that the approach could improve the efficiency and quality of financial services. It also frames the work as relevant to the rapid and steady development of the financial industry.
